neutral_facts.value: The accused, a man, was involved in an incident where a 18-year-old girl sustained burn injuries. The victim, who was alone at her house, was found in flames by her brother. The police inspector recorded an oral statement from the victim, who implicated the accused in pouring kerosene oil on her and setting her on fire with a match-stick. A dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate, which the victim also made, implicating the accused. The victim was later transferred to another hospital where a different Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration stating the incident was an accident caused by a falling chimney. The victim died in the hospital from burn injuries. The prosecution presented medical evidence and witness statements supporting the claim that the death was due to burns, not an accident. The courts below rejected the defense's theory of accidental death, relying on the victim's statements and medical evidence.

quotes.text: The accused, a man, was involved in an incident where a 18-year-old girl sustained burn injuries.
The victim, who was alone at her house, was found in flames by her brother.
The police inspector recorded an oral statement from the victim, who implicated the accused in pouring kerosene oil on her and setting her on fire with a match-stick.
A dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate, which the victim also made, implicating the accused.
The victim was later transferred to another hospital where a different Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration stating the incident was an accident caused by a falling chimney.
The victim died in the hospital from burn injuries.
The prosecution presented medical evidence and witness statements supporting the claim that the death was due to burns, not an accident.
The courts below rejected the defense's theory of accidental death, relying on the victim's statements and medical evidence.

On the basis of the above oral statement, a case No. 63/89 was registered for an offence punishable under Section 307 IPC.
The Sessions Judge had convicted the appellant for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to undergo life imprisonment.
The High Court maintained the conviction.
Appeal dismissed.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the victim's dying declarations, including the oral statement and the first dying declaration recorded by the Magistrate, clearly implicated the accused in the murder. The courts below correctly rejected the defense's theory of accidental death caused by a falling chimney, as the evidence showed the death was due to burn injuries caused by the accused pouring kerosene oil on the victim and setting her on fire.

quotes.text: The prosecution case in nutshell is, Baby a girl of 18 years was residing at Mehkar with her parents, sister and brother.
The doctor in her statement has recorded about 72 per cent burns.

defence_argument.value: The defense argued that the third dying declaration, recorded by the Executive Magistrate, exonerated the accused and stated that the death was accidental, caused by a falling chimney (burning lamp). They contended that the courts below should not have relied on the first two dying declarations due to inconsistencies and the lack of corroboration.

quotes.text: The defence argued that the third dying declaration, recorded by the Executive Magistrate, exonerated the accused and stated that the death was accidental, caused by a falling chimney (burning lamp).
The case put up by the defence that death took place on account of chimney (kerosene lamp) falling on the Baby while she was sleeping and death was by accident, was not accepted.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that each dying declaration must be considered independently on its own merit, and the court must satisfy itself which one reflects the true state of affairs. The court also emphasized that a dying declaration cannot be rejected solely because it is not in question-answer form.

quotes.text: Each dying declaration has to be considered independently on its own merit so as to appreciate its evidentiary value and one cannot be rejected because of the contents of the other.
It is the duty of the court to consider each one of them in its correct perspective and satisfy itself that which one of them reflects the true state of affairs.
